title: Mukati
author: Ssalongo Ssali
desc: Maize ground on a stone or in a mortar, tied up in a leaf and boiled into a solid block or oval — bread made without an oven or a pan.
longDesc: Mukati, known as Maracha bread after the West Nile district, is a maize snack that is boiled rather than baked or fried. The maize is ground on a grinding stone or pounded in a mortar, tied in a leaf, and boiled until it sets into a block or an oval. It is the same principle as a tamale or a Ghanaian kenkey: the leaf is the mould and the pot is the oven, which is exactly what you do in a kitchen with a fire and no oven.
ingredients: Maize, ground on a stone or pounded in a mortar
equipment: Grinding stone, or mortar and pestle
steps: Grind the maize on a stone, or pound it in a mortar.
Tie the ground maize up in a leaf, shaping it into a block or an oval.
Boil the parcels until firm and set.
chefTips: The leaf is the mould. Tie it tightly and the bread takes the shape you gave it; tie it loose and you get a shapeless mass.
A block or an oval is the documented shape, and the shaping happens at the tying stage rather than afterwards.
Boiled, not baked or fried. This is bread made in a pot, which is what you do without an oven.
Grind it on a stone or in a mortar as the source says. The coarseness of stone-ground maize is part of the texture.
No quantities, no water ratio and no boiling time are documented in any source. Those are real gaps and nothing here fills them.
It is named after Maracha district in West Nile, which is where it belongs.
The nearest documented relatives in this collection are ebwanga, UGA030, which is steamed rather than boiled, and the banana-leaf parcels of luwombo. All three use the leaf as a vessel.
Akarafi, UGA105, is the other Lugbara tea-time item and the two go together.
commonMistakes: Using leaves that split in boiling water.
Under-boiling, so the centre stays raw.
Using fine commercial maize meal and expecting the same texture.
Unwrapping it while it is still soft.
sources: Adapted from the Wikipedia article on Lugbara cuisine, which describes Maracha bread or mukati as a maize snack ground on stone or in a mortar, tied in a leaf and boiled into a block or oval shape. That is the entirety of the documented method.
No quantities, no water ratio and no boiling time are given in that source or in any other consulted. None has been estimated.
That article carries only three references, including web archives and blog material on Lugbara culture, so its detail is treated as a lead rather than as established fact.
storage: In its leaf, 2 days at room temperature or 4 refrigerated.
reheating: Boil or steam the parcel again for a few minutes.
healthBenefits: Maize supplies fibre, folate and thiamine.
Boiled in leaf with no added fat at all.
Stone-ground maize retains more of the germ than commercial flour.
culturalNote: Boiling a starch inside a leaf turns up independently in West Africa, Central America and East Asia, and it is the solution a kitchen reaches when it has a fire, a pot and no oven. That West Nile's version is named after a district rather than a technique suggests it is considered local and particular rather than generic.
